name: Dana Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small woodwind ensemble, play clarinet, record practice parts and coach the younger players. I have a master's degree in music and have led rehearsals for thirty years; people call me when a difficult entrance will not settle. The work I like is watching six players start breathing as one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Does leading the group pay steadily?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner cooks at a care home, and our children are grown. The ensemble is skilled but the regional arts charity has frozen our fees for four seasons; my pay is low for a lead player. We rent, have only two weeks of expenses saved after a large dental bill, and few nearby ensembles need another director. I use AI occasionally for draft rehearsal notes after a colleague has tested it, then check the score myself.

I'd say **six wind players** still need a live breath cue.

My partner's **care-home wage** cannot replace all my concert pay.
do: Request **four paid concerts** and written cancellation terms; keep coaching six ensemble players.
Check **AI note drafts** against the score without buying a new tool or spending rent money.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary concert gaps and frozen fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ensemble that a faster rehearsal note is welcome if every player's paid call remains on the sheet. A computer cannot cue six wind players through a breath together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two-week reserve and the charity's frozen fees make a cancelled concert a rent problem already. My partner's regular wage helps, but it cannot replace a whole month of my calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the charity for the next four paid concerts and written cancellation pay, and keep coaching the six current players. In the first year of this mild change I'll continue checking occasional AI note drafts against the score, without buying a new tool or moving money from rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the ordinary gap between paid concerts. A quicker rehearsal note does not raise the charity's frozen concert fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after a cancellation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall cancelled a winter show after the charity had called us in. We received the rehearsal fee but not the performance fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children bridge a fee gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't count our grown children as a payroll. They can come to a concert, but they have their own bills.

I'd seek **written revised fees** before any preparation cut.
think: Practice parts and planning bring **one-third** of my own pay.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot cover an unpaid planning gap.
do: Bring **last-season invoices** to the ensemble committee this month.
Seek **written rehearsal/preparation minimums** if planning fees fall; keep current paid concerts.
Decline **new AI tools** without a paid demo on my owned nameless part, approved local storage/licence and manual playing.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic cut to my own planning pay.
S1.quote: A committee minute is not a fee in our bank account.
fieldNote: Her **high thinking-AI exposure** is in paid planning and practice parts, not only recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the charity which paid practice-part and rehearsal-planning hours software will replace. I'd ask the board to show us revised fees in writing before it cuts anyone's preparation time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice parts and planning bring almost a third of my own pay. The charity may buy less of that work while still expecting me to lead a whole rehearsal, and two weeks saved cannot carry that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll total last season's practice-part and planning invoices and bring them to the ensemble committee. In the first year, if those fees fall, I'll ask for a paid live-rehearsal minimum and written preparation hours before accepting new dates; I'll keep the current paid concerts and use no new AI tool without a paid demonstration on music I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic third of my pay being at risk. A committee minute is not a fee in our bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe AI demonstration require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A demonstration would need to use my own nameless part, a licence allowing paid use and approved local storage. I would play every suggested change and stop if a note moved wrongly or a file left the charity's system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the committee show the board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The committee can show the board how many paid hours the last six arrangements took. I want a written minimum before a new season starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players that thinking AGI by 2028 could arrange practice parts before a robot plays clarinet. Clarinet-playing robots follow around 2031, so I would ask for signed live ensemble calls now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the charity to stop buying practice parts and paid planning in 2028, taking nearly a third of my pay. Live concerts might also shrink, but they remain booked for now; the first loss alone strains rent. I wake at night counting the paid calls that would be left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total practice-part and planning fees, ask for signed paid ensemble dates and request an actual pension estimate before discussing retirement at 60. In the first year after 2028, if paid live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid conservatory ensemble-coach role only if it accepts my master's degree and directing history, pays for live human rehearsal coaching, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the last bus runs; I'll keep present concerts and coaching until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the expected loss of nearly a third of my pay against two weeks saved. I can search, but there are few local director posts and no one has offered me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a conservatory job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the conservatory has not posted a coach vacancy. A former colleague there is not a paid opening with hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need the actual pension estimate before reducing paid work. A master's degree and a birthday cannot pay rent together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the charity that five years to AGI by 2031 gives us time to bargain for paid live rehearsal leadership. Playing robots follow around 2034; a written fee for coaching real players matters before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cut arrangement fees before 2031. I could lead more paid rehearsals, but only if the charity books them rather than assuming my senior title includes free preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll propose a two-year written agreement with a minimum paid live rehearsal, preparation rate and cancellation fee for the six-player ensemble. In the first year after 2031, if practice-part and planning fees end, I'll keep the actually booked paid concerts and ask the ensemble committee to compare the charity's calls with that agreement; if live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid conservatory coaching role only if my master's and directing experience qualify, live human ensemble coaching is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about arrangement work fading, with an agreement giving some control. A proposed rehearsal is not income until the charity signs a paid call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the board agreed to the schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the board has not agreed to two years. I'll put only signed paid dates in the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the committee enforce?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The committee can document any missed minimum against the written agreement. It cannot order the charity to hire me for a concert it cancels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players that ten years to AGI by 2036 is time to read actual pension figures and a real paid rehearsal plan. Clarinet-playing robots follow around 2039, but a birthday cannot sign a concert call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need conductor and teaching fees. Two weeks saved now and an unknown pension do not make a stopping date safe, even with a decade's warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a two-year written paid rehearsal plan. I'll save ten percent of each extra cleared chamber concert fee after rent, food and clarinet repairs toward two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid leading and teaching while booked; if live pay falls and my actual pension estimate leaves a gap, I'll seek a posted paid conservatory coach role only if my master's and directing qualify, live human rehearsal coaching is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces losses and the bus works, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a long run of low fees, even with time to plan. A pension statement will tell me more than another decade of hopeful posters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra concert pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra chamber concert pays, nothing from that source goes into savings. I will not transfer rent money to make the target look reached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen a pension figure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not seen a pension figure. I'll compare the actual amount with rent and signed calls before cutting work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-part and planning pay could end before another senior role opens. Signed ensemble dates, an actual pension estimate and a posted qualified coaching job with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the lead player to prepare a rehearsal before anyone arrives. A master's degree cannot turn unpaid preparation into rent.

headlineQuote: A master's degree cannot turn unpaid preparation into rent.
portrait: Dana is a **58-year-old ensemble lead** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
Her **low pay**, two-week reserve and few nearby posts persist despite excellent clarinet skill and senior responsibility.
She uses **AI occasionally** for draft notes, checked against the score, while bargaining for paid preparation.
She requests **actual pension figures** and keeps paid leading until a qualified signed replacement offer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end almost a third of Dana's pay from practice parts and planning.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed ensemble calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualified coaching with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
